Day 1Saturday 20 June
Arrival

Arrival via Colomares Castle

Your Andalucían adventure begins at Málaga airport. Pick up the rental car and head west along the A-7 coastal motorway. After about 25–30 minutes, exit at Benalmádena and follow signs up to Colomares Castle — an extraordinary monument built entirely by hand between 1987 and 1994 as a tribute to Christopher Columbus by local doctor Esteban Martín Martín. It looks like a fantasy medieval fortress, blending Gothic, Byzantine and Mudéjar architectural styles into one extraordinary building. Every turret and archway demands to be explored, and the children will want to climb everything in sight. Inside the grounds is the world's smallest church, at just under 2 square metres, listed in the Guinness Book of Records — it seats just two people. Allow about an hour for the visit. After your visit, rejoin the AP-4 heading west and continue to Cádiz — roughly another 1h 45 min. Arrive mid-afternoon, check in, settle the children, and find somewhere nearby for your first evening tapas. The old town is best explored on foot; there's no better introduction than wandering without a plan on the first evening.

Aim to arrive before 1pm — the castle closes 2pm–5pm in summer. Entrance €3 adults / €2 children, bought at the door. No booking needed.

Day 2Sunday 21 June
Rest / Beach

Cádiz Beaches & Parque Genovés

A gentle first full day to find your bearings in the old city — no excursions, no driving, just the pleasure of being in one of Europe's most atmospheric cities. Start the morning at La Caleta, the small beach tucked inside the historic centre between the Castillo de Santa Catalina and the Castillo de San Sebastián. It's the most sheltered and manageable beach in Cádiz for young children — calm, compact, and surrounded by history. James Bond fans will recognise it: several scenes from Die Another Day were filmed here. In the afternoon, walk north along the seafront promenade to Parque Genovés, widely considered one of the most beautiful urban parks in Andalucía. The children can climb the waterfall, explore the shaded paths, and play on the playground while you have a coffee at the café. End the day with a wander through the La Viña neighbourhood for evening tapas — this is the most local, most spirited barrio in Cádiz, home to the city's famous carnival traditions and some of its best tapas bars.

No agenda and no car needed — everything is within easy walking distance from the old town.

Day 3Monday 22 June
Excursion

El Puerto de Santa María — Train Out, Boat Back

Leave the car at the hotel and walk to Cádiz train station for one of the most enjoyable days of the trip. The Cercanías train to El Puerto de Santa María takes just 23 minutes and runs every 30–40 minutes — buy tickets at the machine for a couple of euros each. El Puerto is a beautiful, unhurried Andalucían town with a rich seafaring history, far less visited than Cádiz itself. Start with the Castillo de San Marcos, a 13th-century Moorish fortress built on the site of an earlier mosque — it's compact and fascinating. Then head to the Ribera del Marisco waterfront for a long, indulgent seafood lunch. This kilometre-long strip of fish restaurants is one of the finest in the entire province, specialising in the incredibly fresh shellfish, prawns and langoustines pulled from the bay. Don't rush — this is the kind of lunch that lasts two hours. In the afternoon, walk to the catamaran terminal and take the boat back to Cádiz. The 30-minute crossing offers a perspective on the city that no road can match: as you approach from the water, the white skyline of the old city rises dramatically from the bay — the golden dome of the Cathedral glinting in the late afternoon sun. It's a genuinely memorable arrival, especially for the children.

Buy the return catamaran ticket on arrival in El Puerto — popular evening crossings sell out in high season. If the bay is choppy, the train back is fine. ~€5 per person each way.

Day 4Tuesday 23 June
Rest + Meeting · 10:30–11:30

Cádiz Culture Day

After the morning meeting, the rest of the day is yours to explore the old town at a relaxed pace — there's no driving and no agenda. Torre Tavira is the tallest of Cádiz's historic watchtowers and home to the city's famous camera obscura, which projects a live, moving image of the city onto a curved white screen in a darkened room. The effect is genuinely magical — you can see people walking, cars moving, boats in the bay — all in real time from above. Children find it fascinating. Book a time slot in advance online; sessions run throughout the day. From Torre Tavira, it's a short walk to the Cathedral. The baroque golden dome is one of the defining sights of Andalucía — visible from kilometres out at sea, it was built between 1722 and 1838 and funded by trade with the Americas, which is why locals sometimes call it the Cathedral of the Americas. The tower is climbed by ramp rather than stairs, making it accessible for everyone including young children, and the views from the top over the city and the Atlantic are extraordinary. The combined ticket covers the tower, the crypt (where composer Manuel de Falla is buried), and the cathedral museum.

Book Torre Tavira time slots online in advance — capacity is limited and fills quickly in summer. Pay €8 per person on arrival.

Day 5Wednesday 24 June
Long Day

Ronda via Arcos de la Frontera

Leave by 8:30am — this is the most dramatic day of the entire trip and deserves an early start. The first stop, about 30 minutes from Cádiz, is Arcos de la Frontera — one of Andalucía's most spectacular white villages, perched on a sheer cliff edge above the Guadalete river gorge. Park at the bottom and walk up through the narrow whitewashed lanes to the Plaza del Cabildo, where the views across the gorge and the patchwork plains below are breathtaking. Allow about an hour to explore — the church of Santa María de la Asunción at the clifftop is worth a look inside. Back in the car, continue east for about an hour through the Sierra de Cádiz to Ronda. This ancient city, divided by the dramatic El Tajo gorge, is one of the most visited sights in Andalucía — and for good reason. The Puente Nuevo bridge, built between 1751 and 1793, spans 120 metres above the gorge floor. Walking across it and looking straight down into the ravine is genuinely vertiginous and will captivate even the youngest traveller. Explore the old Moorish town on one side of the gorge, visit the Plaza de Toros (one of the oldest and most beautiful bullrings in Spain), and have a long lunch at one of the restaurants with terrace views over the mountains and the plain stretching south towards Cádiz. Leave Ronda by 4:30pm at the latest for a comfortable drive back through the Sierra de Cádiz — the evening light on the white villages is beautiful.

Wednesday is a weekday — noticeably fewer tourists than at weekends. Leave early, take your time, and be back in Cádiz by 7pm.

Day 6Thursday 25 June
Rest / Beach

Playa Victoria & Mercado Central

A restorative day after the long drive to Ronda. Start the morning at the Mercado Central de Abastos — Cádiz's magnificent covered fish market, open every morning except Sunday. This is where the city's chefs, restaurants and home cooks do their shopping, and the atmosphere is wonderful: gleaming tuna the size of a person, mountains of prawns and coquinas, every variety of local shellfish on beds of ice, and vendors calling out the morning's catch. The building itself, from 1838, is a handsome neoclassical structure. Spend half an hour browsing before heading to Playa Victoria. This long, wide sandy beach stretches along the south side of the city for about two kilometres — it's a completely different experience to La Caleta: more open, more spacious, and with the full force of the Atlantic in front of you. A row of chiringuitos (beach bars) lines the promenade, serving cold beers, fresh fish and the local speciality of papas aliñás (warm potato salad). Spend the whole afternoon here — this is exactly what a holiday should feel like.

The market is best between 9am and noon. Playa Victoria is a 20-minute walk or short taxi from the old town.

Day 7Friday 26 June
Rest + Meeting · 13:30–14:30

Old Town Morning & Free Afternoon

The meeting falls right in the middle of the day, so the plan is simple: a relaxed morning on both sides of it, with no pressure to be anywhere. In the morning, explore El Pópulo — the oldest neighbourhood in Cádiz, a dense labyrinth of Roman-era lanes tucked behind the Cathedral. Unlike the broader tourist areas of the old town, El Pópulo has a genuine local atmosphere: small squares where older residents sit in the shade, neighbourhood bars that open early, and the remnants of the medieval city walls woven into the fabric of the buildings. The Arco de los Blancos and the Arco de la Rosa are two of the original medieval gateways still standing. Alternatively, revisit La Caleta for a morning swim if the children prefer. After the meeting, the afternoon is entirely free — use it however the family votes. A good option is to find a restaurant you've been meaning to try for a long leisurely late lunch, then a slow evening walk along the Paseo Marítimo watching the light change over the Atlantic. Sunsets from the city walls are exceptional in late June.

No car needed today. The meeting is central and everything else is on foot.

↗ El Pópulo guide
Day 8Saturday 28 June
Rest / Beach

Free Day — At Your Own Pace

A free day with no fixed agenda — use it however the family needs. After a busy week of excursions and long drives, this is a chance to slow down completely. Revisit whichever beach won the family vote — La Caleta for the sheltered, historic feel or Playa Victoria for space and chiringuitos. Have a long, unhurried seafood lunch somewhere you've been meaning to try: Cádiz has an exceptional restaurant scene centred on its extraordinary local fish. In the evening, take a walk along the city walls at the western tip of the old town — the Baluarte de la Candelaria and the Campo del Sur promenade offer the best sunset views in the city, with the Atlantic stretching away to the west and the golden dome of the Cathedral behind you. Cádiz is at its very best when you're not in a hurry — the old city is small enough to wander entirely without a plan, and on a warm June evening with the light fading slowly over the sea, there are few better places in Spain to simply exist.

No agenda today. Let the family decide. Cádiz rewards slow, unplanned wandering.

↗ Cádiz city walls walk
Day 9Sunday 28 June
Excursion

Jerez de la Frontera

Head to Jerez — the spiritual home of sherry wine and Andalucían horsemanship, about 45 minutes from Cádiz. The morning centrepiece is the Royal Andalusian School of Equestrian Art (Real Escuela Andaluza del Arte Ecuestre), one of the finest equestrian schools in the world. The morning training sessions, which run on weekdays and Saturdays, offer an intimate view of the Carthusian horses and their riders practising the complex dressage movements known as the 'Haute École' — pirouettes, piaffe, passage — in the stunning 19th-century covered riding hall. The horses are pure white and the discipline extraordinary; children and adults are equally captivated. Note that the school is closed on Sundays, so this excursion is on Saturday (Day 8) — if the schedule has shifted, confirm in advance. After the equestrian school, walk through Jerez's handsome old town: the Alcázar with its Moorish baths and mosque, the cathedral, and the sherry bodegas that line the streets. González Byass (Tío Pepe) is the most architecturally impressive and family-friendly for a bodega visit — the vast cathedral-like warehouses filled with thousands of barrels, many signed by visiting heads of state and celebrities, are genuinely spectacular. Have lunch in the old town before driving back to Cádiz.

Book equestrian school tickets online in advance — sessions sell out. Drive ~45 min from Cádiz.

Day 10Monday 29 June
Rest + Meeting · 10:30–11:30

Parque Genovés & Beach Afternoon

A gentle morning before the meeting, with the afternoon free for a final lazy beach day before the last run of excursions. Parque Genovés is one of the best places in the old town to spend the morning with children — it's right in the centre, beautifully maintained, and has a proper playground, a climbable artificial waterfall, shaded paths through exotic plantings, and a café. After the meeting, head to whichever beach the family prefers — La Caleta for the sheltered, historic setting or Playa Victoria for the wider open beach with more facilities. This is your last proper beach afternoon before the two final excursion days, so make the most of it: a long lunch at a chiringuito, an afternoon in the water, and an easy evening in the old town.

All on foot — no car needed. Meeting is in the city centre.

↗ La Caleta↗ Playa Victoria
Day 11Tuesday 30 June
Excursion

Bolonia Beach & Roman Ruins

Drive south along the Costa de la Luz — one of the most beautiful and unspoilt stretches of Atlantic coastline in Spain — to Baelo Claudia, about an hour from Cádiz. This is one of the most complete and best-preserved Roman towns in the entire Iberian Peninsula, and the setting is extraordinary: a full Roman forum, basilica, three temples dedicated to Juno, Minerva and Jupiter, a theatre, thermal baths, and the remains of the factories where the Romans produced garum — the fermented fish sauce that was exported across the Empire — all sitting directly on the beach, with the Atlantic surf visible beyond the ruins. Entry is free for EU passport holders. Allow 2–3 hours to explore properly; the on-site museum provides excellent context. The children can play archaeologist in the ruins before everyone retreats to the beach restaurants for lunch. The afternoon is spent on Playa de Bolonia itself — one of the most spectacular beaches in Andalucía. Wide, wild and backed by enormous sand dunes (the Duna de Bolonia rises 30 metres), it has a completely different character from the town beaches in Cádiz: raw, Atlantic, and magnificent. Note that Baelo Claudia is closed on Mondays — hence the Tuesday scheduling.

Closed Mondays — Tuesday is correct. Free for EU passport holders. Drive ~1 hour from Cádiz. Bring sunscreen — the dunes offer no shade.

Day 12Wednesday 1 July
Excursion

Seville

Leave by 8:30am for the grandest day of the trip. Seville is 1h 15 min by road or 1h 40 min by train (which runs hourly and removes all parking headaches — recommended). Start with the Real Alcázar, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most breathtaking buildings in Europe: a royal palace complex of extraordinary Moorish and Renaissance architecture, with tiled courtyards, ornate arches, elaborate gardens with fountains and orange trees, and underground baths that feel unchanged since the 14th century. Pedro I's palace, built in the 1360s by Moorish craftsmen from Granada, is the centrepiece — its interiors are among the finest examples of Mudéjar art in existence. Book tickets well in advance: July queues without a pre-booked slot can mean two hours of waiting or being turned away entirely. After the Alcázar, walk through the Barrio de Santa Cruz — the old Jewish quarter, a labyrinth of whitewashed lanes, hidden plazas, orange trees and flower-draped balconies — for lunch at one of the terrace restaurants. In the afternoon, the Cathedral and Giralda tower round out the day perfectly: the Cathedral is the largest Gothic church in the world, and the Giralda tower (the former minaret of the mosque, converted in the 16th century) is climbed entirely by ramp, making it accessible for everyone. The views from the top over the rooftops of Seville are spectacular. Leave by 4:30–5pm.

Wednesday is the best weekday — fewest crowds. Book Alcázar tickets as far in advance as possible. Consider the train to avoid Seville city-centre parking.

Day 13Thursday 2 July
Departure

Departure — Cádiz to Málaga Airport

Check out and drive back to Málaga Airport along the A-7/AP-4 — approximately 2 hours in normal summer traffic. Leave by 9am at the latest to be comfortable for most morning or midday flights; if you have an early flight, allow extra time. Return the rental car at the terminal (follow signs to the car rental return area, which is well signposted at Málaga Airport), check in, and depart. If time allows before the drive, walk down to the seafront one last time for a final coffee and pastry — the café terraces along the Paseo Marítimo are the perfect send-off. Cádiz has a way of making you want to come back.

Leave by 9am at the latest. Allow extra time for summer traffic on the A-7/AP-4. The car rental return at Málaga is well signposted.
